Antibiotic time bomb

By: Bernadette Maguire | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Antibiotic resistance has been described as one of the biggest global threats - even more deadly than the threat of terrorism.

Summary:
Already 700 000 people die globally due to antibiotic resistance. In 10 or 20 years time, if nothing is done, we'll see people dying from simple infections.

In South Africa the devastating effects are already being felt....there's been an increase in superbugs and antibiotic resistance. Helene van der Merwe was one of the first people to be impacted. She lost her 35 year old son when he contracted a superbug in hospital, antibiotics failed and sadly he passed away. Ian Samson was luckier, he also contracted a hospital infection and was on an IV drip for a week and then several courses of antibiotics before the infection finally cleared up. He says it was frightening,

Antimicrobial resistance is a global threat.

It happens when organisms are able to survive medicines aimed to destroy them.
Bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics, viruses to antivirals and parasites to drugs like antimalarials.
The World Health Organization says 150,000 deaths a year are caused by multi-drug resistant tuberculosis.
If we don't take action, then we may all be back in an almost 19th Century environment where infections kill us as a result of routine operations. We won't be able to do a lot of our cancer treatments or organ transplants.
Pharmaceutical companies need to be encouraged to develop new drugs, because the manufacture of antibiotics was not viewed as profitable.

We haven't had a new class of antibiotics since the late 80s and there are very few antibiotics in the pipeline of the big pharmaceutical companies that develop and make drugs.
We haven't as a society globally incentivised making antibiotics. It's quite simple - if they make something to treat high blood pressure or diabetes and it works, we will use it on our patients every day.
Whereas antibiotics will only be used for a week or two when they're needed, and then they have a limited life span because of resistance developing anyway.




Further information:
Dricky van Rooyen is a cop. She's tough and works with the bomb squad. But she'd been facing a debiliating infection since April this year. She's unable to work, lives in pain and can't seem to get rid of the infection that is eating away at her nerves in her back. The reason: She has an extreme antibiotic resistant hospital acquired infection or superbug called pseundominae. The problem is no-one wants to take responsibility and even medical negligence lawyers don't know how to deal with these cases. But the reality is that they are on the rise and its time we deal with them.

In PE Tracy van Biljon's mom is in the same boat, she's also battling a hospital acquired superbug. It's been months and she can't shake it.

But its not just superbugs. Ian Sampson got a routine infection, couldn't shake it and had to spend weeks on a series on antibiotics and antibiotic drips.

These are not isolated incidents. It's part of a global pandemic that will in the coming years see thousand of South Africans marching to their graves if nothing is done.

Dr Jennifer Coetzee a local antibiotic expert from Lancet laboratories says she sees weekly evidence of antibiotic resistance in the labs. There used to be antibiotics that worked for carbopenem enterobacteraceae but now the bacteria has morphed to survive it. This is one of the biggest problems - bacteria can morph in a matter of days but it takes us years to develop new antibiotics. Already one South East Asian child dies every 5 minutes due to resistant bacteria.

The problem of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, already an “apocalyptic” threat, is poised to get worse. The reason? The world’s hunger for meat.
In the first estimate of its kind, researchers calculate that farmers globally feed 63,000 tonnes of antibiotics to chickens, pigs and cattle every year – and that will climb by 67 per cent, to 106,000 tonnes, by 2030.
Antibiotics fed to livestock encourage the evolution of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, which have repeatedly been linked to human infections.
Most of the increase in antibiotic use is expected to be in middle-income countries, but once resistant bacteria appear, they can spread round the world. The problem is getting worse as people become more prosperous and eat more meat and dairy. For example, Tim Robinson of the International Livestock Research Institute in Nairobi, Kenya, and his colleagues calculate that the total biomass of livestock around the world now outstrips that of people, illustrating the size of the demand.

We will also include comment from Maryn Mckenna whose tedtalks video on the subject went viral.

Press Release:


Antibiotics Resistance
It’s an arms race between mutating organisms and pharmaceutical companies – and we’re losing the battle fast. By 2050, superbugs will kill up to ten million people every year. These deadly organisms - often acquired while people are recovering in hospital ICUs – now survive the antibiotic cocktails long used in trying to destroy them. Could cell phone use in hospitals be worsening the spread? Carte Blanche investigates a phenomenon described as deadlier than the threat of terrorism.


Script:


Script: Antibiotic Time Bomb

VO: 8”
It may sound alarmist but around the world healthcare workers agree that antibiotic resistance could pose a greater risk than terrorism.

Guy Richards:
I think it may well be a bigger threat than terrorism in the long term. Currently we are sitting in a situation in the intensive care units which represent the pinnacle of therapy overall where sometimes we have organisms that are resistant to all known antibiotics.

VO: 14”
In 2014 700 000 deaths were recorded globally as a result of antimicrobial resistance – that’s according to a project commissioned by the British government.

DG:
It knows no boundaries – it doesn’t need a passport, it doesn’t need a visa. It cuts across all levels and all sectors of society.

VO
Reports suggest by 2050 the figure will rise to 10 million deaths annually - more than the death toll to cancer and diabetes combined.

Bongani link: 15 sec
One of the biggest problems is hospital acquired infections with known as superbugs. Now these organisms are extremely resistant to antibiotics especially when they haven’t been treated correctly. showing a resistance to antibiotics. But the real issue is when they become resistant to last resort antibiotics then results can be deadly.

Prof Richards:
It’s klebsiella, it’s entrobacter, its ecoli, proteus, serratia, its morganella, salmonella and citrobacter are the major ones that are able to produce these enzymes that then overcome the ability of the antibiotic to kill them.

VO:
Maritsa Balanco has devastating first hand experience. Her husband Frik was her closest friend, her confidant. Then he fell ill.

Maritsa:
He had a stomach ulcer and they sent him to a general ward. There I sat with him through the whole night.

VO:
Three days later his condition deteriorated. He was transferred to ICU and that’s where she discovered he had contracted a cocktail of superbugs.

Maritsa:
On one of the days I secretly went through his files. There I saw written klebsiella and I went to google to see what it is as I didn’t get answers on what was wrong with my husband. When I looked through I saw staphylococcus virus too.

VO: 3”
Frik spent six weeks in ICU before he passed away.

Bongani link: 16 sec
Statistics vary on the subject. Certainly hospitals are reluctant to admit that infections are rampant and currently some say the infection rate is somewhere between 14 and 50%.

VO: 14”
Dricky van Rooyen says if she had known the risks she would never have gone for a back operation to release a pinched nerve in April this year. The operation went well but 10 days later she realized something was wrong.

Dricky:
We saw that the plasters were brown. There was something wrong and when we went to the doctor on the 14th day he took swabs and he said no I have got a hospital virus.

VO:
She was re-admitted for intravenous antibiotics and needed several follow up courses.

Dricky:
But my wound wouldn’t heal.

VO:
The bacteria ravaged the site of the wound creating extensive damage and leaving her in tremendous pain.

Dricky:
It feels like somebody is taking a knife and pushing the knife the whole time in your back. That’s the feeling. I cannot sleep on one of my sides because that’s where the pain is.

VO:
This surge in microbial resistant organisms is being linked directly to an increase in antibiotic consumption says Dr Kim Faure from the Centre for Disease Dynamics, Economics and Policy.

Kim:
So we are using more antibiotics than the rest of the developing world which means that we have the potential of developing as much resistance as the developing world. We are sitting somewhere between India and Europe when it comes to resistance in certain organisms.

Bongani:
Should we be afraid?

Kim:
We should be. I think we should all know that every time we take an antibiotic we are not just impacting our own organisms in our own body and generating resistance for ourselves and potentially getting to a point where we can’t use an antibiotic but we are also potentially spreading organisms that are resistant to other people.

VO:
And the old saying is true prevention is still better than cure.


DG:
Infection control in our hospitals and health facilities must be everybody’s business

Guy Richards:
Bacteria don’t have wings. They cannot fly from one patient to the other. They get carried there and the prime means of carrying them is on hands.

VO:
A critical link in the infection chain came from an unexpected quarter. A 15 year old school girl Toni- Ann Black decided to look at the spread of hospital acquired infections.

Toni:
I was job shadowing at one of the hospitals and I noticed a lot of the healthcare workers were using their cellular phones. For verification purposes but It just struck me as odd. They would use their phone, wash their hands, use their phone again and touch a patient then wash their hands again.

VO:
Tony put together a questionaire and found that only 14% of healthcare workers sterilised their phones.

Toni:
30% of the bacteria on your cellular phone is transferred to your hand in a single touch. Which I found was kind of intriguing and rather scary.

VO:
Ironically Tony’s research showed that if cleaning protocols were not done correctly there would be an increase in the bacteria on the phones. That’s when she came up with an incentivized scheme: a charging station for cell phones using UV lights for sterilisation.

Toni:
What it found is in terms of the sterilization process if healthcare workers left their cellular phones in the docking station for 10 minutes there was a 99.9% decrease in the bacteria on the cellular phones and this decrease persisted six hours after at 98.8% decrease.

DG:
That’s a welcome innovative idea. I think we’d like to invite them so we can understand it better and include them in join us to fight any antimicrobial resistance.

VO:
Last year her invention saw her winning 3rd prize in microbiology at the prestigious International Science and Engineering Fair in Los Angeles.
While it’s important to manage infection control – we need to cut down on antibiotics too. Estimates suggest a 60% increase in antibiotic usage in the last 10 years – a lot of that is due to food production.

Kim:
The majority of the antibiotics used in the world are actually in agriculture and they are used for growth promotion and they are used in big herds of animals to prevent them from getting ill. And the more we use it there for organisms that are potentially human organisms as well we can transfer that resistance to the humans as well.

Prof Richards:
There’s a direct relationship between the development of resistance and the use of those antibiotics in the community.

Bongani link:
It’s now widely accepted that we are fast approaching a post antibiotic era.

VO:
Research and development can’t keep pace with the ever adapting organisms. Some organisms can adapt in a matter of hours while developing new drugs takes years.

Kim:
The pipeline of antibiotics shows that those that are now being created and come out of this innovation system and the research cycle will be very expensive. So we probably can’t afford to have those in the country.

VO:
So does it all come down to the bottom line?

Prof Richards:
You only use them for a relatively short period of time. You can earn a lot more money by making an agent that will treat something like depression where you are going to take it for three years, four years or whatever it happens to be. Or a cholesterol drug that you are going to take for many years. That’s much more likely to make them much more money.

VO:
The after effects of these superbugs can be serious. In order to control the pain caused by the bacteria that damaged the nerves in her back Dricky has an implanted pain management device that blocks pain messages to her brain. But she’s still in agony.

Dricky:
It’s much more than before the operation because before the operation it was only the nerve system that got stuck, now it’s the wounds that are sore, the back is sore. Sot its about 70 or 80% more than before I went for the operation.

VO:
The former marathon runner says its cost her medical aid R100 000 and she’s had to fit some of the bills too.

Dricky:
Approximately out of my own pocket about R10 000.

VO:
Maritsa plans to sue but she needs Frik’s hospital file.

Maritsa:
The lawyer sent letters, I had two different lawyers sending letters, Till now I still haven’t received his hospital file.

VO:
Medical negligence lawyers are loathe to take on these cases.

Dricky
I went to three attorneys all of them told me I must prove that the hospital gave me the bacteria. So I must prove the hospital is wrong. They didn’t want to take my case.

VO:
Professor Richards says it’s a catch 22 situation.

Prof Richards:
So you needed to have that tube put in your throat, in the first place to ventilate you, but that tube increases your chances for an infection in your chest. So are you going to say that was negligence or should one then rather just let the patient die? Because if you don’t put the tube in they would die, but if you put the tube in they have an increased potential for developing an infection.

VO:
It’s a big wake-up call for the medical profession who can’t deny we’re facing a healthcare tsunami. In response the DG has set up an antibiotic stewardship programme.

DG:
That will ensure that we’ve got clinical guidelines that enforce prescribing habits.

VO:
Soon there’ll be a lot more scrutiny before you get that script.

Prof Richards:
We are also moving towards a situation in which we are going to require a licence to prescribe antibiotics. Meaning that a doctor may not just because they have qualified as a doctor, prescribe antibiotics.

VO:
Much needed measures that could save patients the pain that Dricky has endured and the intense grief that Maritsa deals with daily.

Maritsa:
I blame myself a lot. I feel like I murdered my husband by leaving him there.




Promos:

Promo 1:
VO: 5 sec

It’s been called a threat bigger than terrorism – that could claim millions of lives.

Guy Richards
Currently we are sitting in a situation in ICU’s where sometimes we have organisms that are resistant to all known antibiotics.


Promo 2:

VO: 6”
Antibiotic resistant organisms or superbugs are playing havoc in hospitals posing a major risk to patients.

Dricky:
When we got to the hospital they saw there was something wrong and they said I had a hospital virus.


Promo 3:

Maritsa Balanco’s husband Frik was admitted to hospital, diagnosed with a stomach ulcer – three days later he was transferred to ICU with a cocktail of deadly superbugs.

And the more we use it there for organisms that are potentially human organisms as well we can transfer that resistance to the humans as well. Prof Richards: There’s a direct relationship between the development of resistance and the use of those antibiotics in the community. Bongani link: It’s now widely accepted that we are fast approaching a post antibiotic era. VO: Research and development can’t keep pace with the ever adapting organisms. Some organisms can adapt in a matter of hours while developing new drugs takes years. Kim: The pipeline of antibiotics shows that those that are now being created and come out of this innovation system and the research cycle will be very expensive. So we probably can’t afford to have those in the country. VO: So does it all come down to the bottom line? Prof Richards: You only use them for a relatively short period of time. You can earn a lot more money by making an agent that will treat something like depression where you are going to take it for three years, four years or whatever it happens to be. Or a cholesterol drug that you are going to take for many years. That’s much more likely to make them much more money. VO: The after effects of these superbugs can be serious. In order to control the pain caused by the bacteria that damaged the nerves in her back Dricky has an implanted pain management device that blocks pain messages to her brain. But she’s still in agony. Dricky: It’s much more than before the operation because before the operation it was only the nerve system that got stuck, now it’s the wounds that are sore, the back is sore. Sot its about 70 or 80% more than before I went for the operation. VO: The former marathon runner says its cost her medical aid R100 000 and she’s had to fit some of the bills too. Dricky: Approximately out of my own pocket about R10 000. VO: Maritsa plans to sue but she needs Frik’s hospital file. Maritsa: The lawyer sent letters, I had two different lawyers sending letters, Till now I still haven’t received his hospital file. VO: Medical negligence lawyers are loathe to take on these cases. Dricky I went to three attorneys all of them told me I must prove that the hospital gave me the bacteria. So I must prove the hospital is wrong. They didn’t want to take my case. VO: Professor Richards says it’s a catch 22 situation. Prof Richards: So you needed to have that tube put in your throat, in the first place to ventilate you, but that tube increases your chances for an infection in your chest. So are you going to say that was negligence or should one then rather just let the patient die? Because if you don’t put the tube in they would die, but if you put the tube in they have an increased potential for developing an infection. VO: It’s a big wake-up call for the medical profession who can’t deny we’re facing a healthcare tsunami. In response the DG has set up an antibiotic stewardship programme. DG: That will ensure that we’ve got clinical guidelines that enforce prescribing habits. VO: Soon there’ll be a lot more scrutiny before you get that script. Prof Richards: We are also moving towards a situation in which we are going to require a licence to prescribe antibiotics. Meaning that a doctor may not just because they have qualified as a doctor, prescribe antibiotics. VO: Much needed measures that could save patients the pain that Dricky has endured and the intense grief that Maritsa deals with daily. Maritsa: I blame myself a lot. I feel like I murdered my husband by leaving him there. Promos: Promo 1: VO: 5 sec It’s been called a threat bigger than terrorism – that could claim millions of lives. Guy Richards Currently we are sitting in a situation in ICU’s where sometimes we have organisms that are resistant to all known antibiotics. Promo 2: VO: 6” Antibiotic resistant organisms or superbugs are playing havoc in hospitals posing a major risk to patients. Dricky: When we got to the hospital they saw there was something wrong and they said I had a hospital virus. Promo 3: Maritsa Balanco’s husband Frik was admitted to hospital, diagnosed with a stomach ulcer – three days later he was transferred to ICU with a cocktail of deadly superbugs.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Antibiotic resistance has been described as one of the biggest global threats - even more deadly than the threat of terrorism.
metadata.Summary: Already 700 000 people die globally due to antibiotic resistance. In 10 or 20 years time, if nothing is done, we'll see people dying from simple infections. In South Africa the devastating effects are already being felt....there's been an increase in superbugs and antibiotic resistance. Helene van der Merwe was one of the first people to be impacted. She lost her 35 year old son when he contracted a superbug in hospital, antibiotics failed and sadly he passed away. Ian Samson was luckier, he also contracted a hospital infection and was on an IV drip for a week and then several courses of antibiotics before the infection finally cleared up. He says it was frightening, Antimicrobial resistance is a global threat. It happens when organisms are able to survive medicines aimed to destroy them. Bacteria can become resistant to antibiotics, viruses to antivirals and parasites to drugs like antimalarials. The World Health Organization says 150,000 deaths a year are caused by multi-drug resistant tuberculosis. If we don't take action, then we may all be back in an almost 19th Century environment where infections kill us as a result of routine operations. We won't be able to do a lot of our cancer treatments or organ transplants. Pharmaceutical companies need to be encouraged to develop new drugs, because the manufacture of antibiotics was not viewed as profitable. We haven't had a new class of antibiotics since the late 80s and there are very few antibiotics in the pipeline of the big pharmaceutical companies that develop and make drugs. We haven't as a society globally incentivised making antibiotics. It's quite simple - if they make something to treat high blood pressure or diabetes and it works, we will use it on our patients every day. Whereas antibiotics will only be used for a week or two when they're needed, and then they have a limited life span because of resistance developing anyway.
metadata.Further information: Dricky van Rooyen is a cop. She's tough and works with the bomb squad. But she'd been facing a debiliating infection since April this year. She's unable to work, lives in pain and can't seem to get rid of the infection that is eating away at her nerves in her back. The reason: She has an extreme antibiotic resistant hospital acquired infection or superbug called pseundominae. The problem is no-one wants to take responsibility and even medical negligence lawyers don't know how to deal with these cases. But the reality is that they are on the rise and its time we deal with them. In PE Tracy van Biljon's mom is in the same boat, she's also battling a hospital acquired superbug. It's been months and she can't shake it. But its not just superbugs. Ian Sampson got a routine infection, couldn't shake it and had to spend weeks on a series on antibiotics and antibiotic drips. These are not isolated incidents. It's part of a global pandemic that will in the coming years see thousand of South Africans marching to their graves if nothing is done. Dr Jennifer Coetzee a local antibiotic expert from Lancet laboratories says she sees weekly evidence of antibiotic resistance in the labs. There used to be antibiotics that worked for carbopenem enterobacteraceae but now the bacteria has morphed to survive it. This is one of the biggest problems - bacteria can morph in a matter of days but it takes us years to develop new antibiotics. Already one South East Asian child dies every 5 minutes due to resistant bacteria. The problem of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, already an “apocalyptic” threat, is poised to get worse. The reason? The world’s hunger for meat. In the first estimate of its kind, researchers calculate that farmers globally feed 63,000 tonnes of antibiotics to chickens, pigs and cattle every year – and that will climb by 67 per cent, to 106,000 tonnes, by 2030. Antibiotics fed to livestock encourage the evolution of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, which have repeatedly been linked to human infections. Most of the increase in antibiotic use is expected to be in middle-income countries, but once resistant bacteria appear, they can spread round the world. The problem is getting worse as people become more prosperous and eat more meat and dairy. For example, Tim Robinson of the International Livestock Research Institute in Nairobi, Kenya, and his colleagues calculate that the total biomass of livestock around the world now outstrips that of people, illustrating the size of the demand. We will also include comment from Maryn Mckenna whose tedtalks video on the subject went viral.
